subject: science

items.q: Which idea is part of Dalton's atomic model?
items.correct: All atoms of one element are identical
items.misconception: An atom has the colour of its element
items.why: Keep two levels apart. What you can see and feel (colour, hardness, wetness, expansion) is a property of the substance; atoms are the tiny particles it is made of, and a single atom does not have those properties.
items.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
items.random_wrong: Atoms can be seen with a light microscope

items.q: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to make water. In Dalton's model, what happens to the hydrogen atoms?
items.correct: They become joined to oxygen atoms
items.misconception: They are destroyed as the hydrogen burns
items.why: Follow the atoms. When a fuel burns, its atoms join with oxygen atoms and many end up in gases you cannot see. No atom is destroyed.
items.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
items.random_wrong: They merge with oxygen into water atoms

items.q: Under a school microscope, sulfur powder looks like tiny yellow grains. Which statement about one grain is correct?
items.correct: It contains a huge number of atoms
items.misconception: It is one single atom of sulfur
items.why: Atoms are many times smaller than anything a light microscope can show. A grain of powder or a speck of dust is made of an enormous number of atoms.
items.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
items.random_wrong: It is made of atoms that are yellow

items.q: The diagram shows the particles of a substance made from X and Y. Someone makes it again with extra Y. What are its particles like now?
items.correct: One X atom joined to two Y atoms
items.misconception: One X atom joined to more Y atoms
items.why: A compound has a fixed ratio of atoms, shown by its formula. Different ratios mean different compounds: CO (carbon monoxide) and CO₂ (carbon dioxide) are two different substances.
items.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
items.random_wrong: Particles that are mixtures of X and Y

items.q: The diagram shows elements X and Y reacting to make a compound. Which statement about the compound is correct?
items.correct: It has new properties of its own
items.misconception: It has the properties of both X and Y
items.why: When elements react, their atoms become chemically joined and a new substance forms, with different properties. Getting the elements back needs another chemical reaction.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: Filtering can split it into X and Y

items.q: Which statement is true of every molecule?
items.correct: It is two or more atoms joined together
items.misconception: It contains atoms of two different elements
items.why: Ask how many different elements are present, not how many atoms are joined. O₂ has only oxygen atoms, so it is an element made of molecules; CO₂ has carbon and oxygen atoms joined, so it is a compound.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: It is just another word for an atom

items.q: Which of these is a compound?
items.correct: Pure water, H₂O
items.misconception: Air in a jar
items.why: A compound needs its elements to be chemically joined in a fixed ratio. If the elements are only mixed, it is a mixture.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: Oxygen gas, O₂

items.q: The diagram shows the particles in a sample of gas. What is the whole sample?
items.correct: An element mixed with a compound
items.misconception: Two elements mixed together
items.why: Look at what is joined to what. Different atoms joined in one particle make a compound; different particles side by side, not joined, make a mixture.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: Two compounds mixed together

items.q: Hydrogen burns, and oxygen helps things burn. They react to make water, which does neither. What does this show?
items.correct: A new substance with its own properties formed
items.misconception: The atoms changed into new water atoms
items.why: A compound's particles are atoms of different elements joined together, not new atoms. In a reaction the atoms stay the same atoms; only what they are joined to changes.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: The atoms were destroyed in the reaction

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.correct: Au
items.misconception: Go
items.why: Learn the Latin-based symbols as a set: Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Pb. For these the symbol does not match the English name.
items.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: AU

items.q: In the formula H₂O, what does the small 2 show?
items.correct: There are two hydrogen atoms
items.misconception: There are two oxygen atoms
items.why: In a formula the number comes after the symbol it counts: H₂ is two hydrogen atoms. Read each symbol together with the small number just after it.
items.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: There are two of every atom

items.q: Methane has the formula CH₄. How many atoms are in one molecule of methane?
items.correct: 5 atoms
items.misconception: 2 atoms
items.why:
Count atoms, not symbols: add up the small numbers, counting 1 for any symbol without a number.

Working: C has no number after it, so there is 1 carbon atom. H₄ means 4 hydrogen atoms. Total = 1 + 4 = 5 atoms.
items.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: 4 atoms
items.working: C has no number after it, so there is 1 carbon atom. H₄ means 4 hydrogen atoms. Total = 1 + 4 = 5 atoms.

items.q: What does the formula N₂ show?
items.correct: Two nitrogen atoms joined to each other
items.misconception: Two nitrogen atoms that are not joined up
items.why: A small (subscript) number counts atoms joined inside one particle. A large number in front counts separate particles.
items.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: A compound that contains nitrogen

items.q: The symbol Co stands for cobalt. What does CO stand for?
items.correct: Carbon and oxygen atoms joined together
items.misconception: Cobalt, written in capital letters
items.why: Every capital letter starts a new symbol. A lower-case letter belongs to the capital before it.
items.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: Carbon and oxygen mixed but not joined

items.q: Carbon monoxide is CO. Carbon dioxide is CO₂. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: CO₂ has one more oxygen atom per molecule
items.misconception: CO₂ is two CO molecules joined together
items.why: A subscript belongs only to the symbol written just before it. A symbol with no subscript stands for one atom.
items.specStatementText: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
items.random_wrong: They are one compound in different amounts

items.q: Some ice in a sealed bag melts, and a little of the water evaporates. What happens to the mass of the bag and its contents?
items.correct: It stays the same, as no particles are lost
items.misconception: It goes down, as liquids weigh less than solids
items.why: In a change of state no particles are made or lost; they are only arranged differently. The mass stays the same.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
items.random_wrong: It goes up, as ice floats, so water is heavier

items.q: In an open beaker, 2.0 g of calcium carbonate (chalk) reacts with 50.0 g of acid. Carbon dioxide escapes, and 51.1 g is left. What mass of carbon dioxide escaped?
items.why:
Gases are matter: their particles have mass. Weigh a sealed container before and after a gas is made inside it and the mass is the same.

Working: Total mass at the start = 50.0 g + 2.0 g = 52.0 g. Mass lost = 52.0 g − 51.1 g = 0.9 g. The mass lost is the carbon dioxide that escaped into the air.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
items.working: Total mass at the start = 50.0 g + 2.0 g = 52.0 g. Mass lost = 52.0 g − 51.1 g = 0.9 g. The mass lost is the carbon dioxide that escaped into the air.

items.q: The diagram shows the particles before and after a reaction in a sealed container. What happens to the total mass?
items.correct: It stays the same, as the same atoms are there
items.misconception: It goes down, as there are fewer particles
items.why: Count atoms, not molecules. If the same atoms are there before and after, the total mass is the same, however they are grouped.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
items.random_wrong: It goes down, as some atoms were used up

items.q: Magnesium is heated in a crucible open to the air until it has all turned into white magnesium oxide. None of the powder escapes. What happens to the mass of the crucible and contents?
items.correct: It goes up, as oxygen from the air joins on
items.misconception: It goes up, as its atoms turn into heavier atoms
items.why: A compound's particles are atoms of different elements joined together, not new atoms. In a reaction the atoms stay the same atoms; only what they are joined to changes.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
items.random_wrong: It goes down, as some magnesium burns away

items.q: The diagram shows the particles as sugar dissolves in water. The beaker is on a balance. What happens to the balance reading?
items.correct: It stays the same, as the sugar is still there
items.misconception: It goes down, as the sugar has disappeared
items.why: Not being able to see the sugar does not mean it has gone. Its particles are still there, so the mass of the solution equals the mass of water plus sugar.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions
items.random_wrong: It goes down, as dissolved sugar weighs nothing

items.q: In Dalton's model, what happens if you keep cutting a piece of copper into smaller and smaller bits?
items.correct: You reach atoms that cannot be split
items.misconception: You can keep cutting smaller bits for ever
items.why: The particle model applies to every substance in every state. A solid grain is a huge number of particles packed closely together.
items.specStatementText: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
items.random_wrong: You reach tiny orange, bendy copper atoms

items.q: Can a compound be split into its elements by filtering or with a magnet?
items.correct: No. The atoms in a compound are chemically joined, so splitting a compound into its elements needs a chemical reaction.
items.misconception: A compound can be separated into its elements by a physical method, such as filtering, boiling or using a magnet, just like a mixture.
items.why: Physical methods separate substances that are only mixed. A compound is one substance; its elements are chemically joined, so only a chemical reaction can split it.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Are 'atom' and 'molecule' two words for the same thing?
items.correct: No. An atom is the smallest particle of an element. A molecule is two or more atoms joined together.
items.misconception: 'Atom' and 'molecule' (and sometimes 'element') are interchangeable words for 'a tiny particle', so a molecule is just one atom.
items.why: Use the words carefully: atoms are the building blocks; molecules are atoms joined together; an element is a substance made of one type of atom.
items.specStatementText: differences between atoms, elements and compounds

items.q: When salt dissolves in water, does it make a compound with the water?
items.correct: No. Salt water is a mixture. The amount of salt can vary, and evaporating the water gives the salt back unchanged.
items.misconception: When a solid dissolves, it joins with the water to make a new compound, so salt water is a compound.
items.why: Dissolving is not a chemical reaction. The salt and water particles are mixed, not joined, so salt water is a mixture.

items.q: Is the symbol for gold Ag?
items.correct: No. Gold is Au (from aurum). Ag is silver (from argentum).
items.misconception: The symbol for gold is Ag (and silver's is Au).
items.why: Link each symbol to its Latin name: Au, aurum, gold; Ag, argentum, silver.

items.q: In CH₄, does carbon count when it has no number after it?
items.correct: Yes. A symbol with no number stands for one atom. CH₄ has 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms, 5 atoms in total.
items.misconception: When counting atoms, only symbols with a number are counted (or a symbol without a number counts as zero), so CH₄ has 4 atoms.
items.why: Every symbol stands for at least one atom. Write in an invisible 1 for any symbol without a number before you add up.

items.q: Is ice lighter than water because it floats?
items.correct: No. Ice floats because it is less dense: the same mass takes up more space. A piece of ice and the water it melts into have the same mass.
items.misconception: Heavier means denser: a denser substance has more mass, so a change that makes something denser (or less dense) changes its mass.
items.why: Mass is how much matter there is; density is how much mass is packed into each cm³. A change that alters density, such as melting or dissolving, does not change the total mass.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

items.q: When working out the mass of gas lost, do you need the masses of all the reactants?
items.correct: Yes. The starting mass is the total of everything that was weighed at the start; the mass of gas lost is that total minus the mass at the end.
items.misconception: The mass of gas lost is the final mass compared with just one of the starting masses (for example the liquid), leaving out a solid that was added.
items.why: Add up every mass at the start first. Then compare that total with the mass at the end.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

items.q: Once sugar has dissolved, is it still there but weightless?
items.correct: No. The sugar is still there and every sugar particle keeps its mass, so the solution weighs as much as the water and sugar did together.
items.misconception: A dissolved substance is still present but weighs nothing (or less), because it is floating or held up in the water.
items.why: Every particle has mass wherever it is. Dissolved sugar particles are still in the beaker, so their mass is still on the balance.
items.specStatementText: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions

items.q: When chalk fizzes in acid, does all of the chalk turn into the gas?
items.correct: No. Only some of the chalk's atoms end up in the carbon dioxide; the rest stay in the beaker in new substances. So the gas has less mass than the chalk.
items.misconception: In a fizzing reaction the solid turns completely into the gas, so all of the solid's mass leaves as gas.
items.why: Follow the atoms. Only some of the chalk's atoms leave as carbon dioxide; the others stay in the beaker. Work out the gas lost from the masses: total at the start minus the mass at the end.
